setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. At the start of the shift, {lead|the} quickly explains a rush job to you and two coworkers.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are in a quick huddle where {lead|the} explains today's rush job.
pressure: {Lead|the} says the team needs to get moving in two minutes.
{coworker3} whispers that it will all make sense once you start.
detail: The huddle is happening next to the time clock.
Two other coworkers are listening too.

tiers.1: A safety warning you did not fully hear has to be cleared up first.
tiers.2: Signs that a teammate disagrees are worth raising while everyone is still together.
tiers.3: A missing detail you need for the job should be confirmed before you start.
tiers.4: Losing track of the instructions calls for a recap before work begins.
tiers.5: Checking your understanding is useful once the gaps are filled.

fact: Over the noise, you only partly heard a warning {lead|the} gave about {equipment|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} also handed out the warning about {equipment|the} in writing.
issues.done: the warning was already given in writing
issues.short: the warning you only partly heard
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to repeat the warning about {equipment|the} before you start.
issues.reason: A safety warning only protects you if you heard all of it. Asking now takes seconds.
issues.lesson: If you did not fully hear a safety warning, ask for it again before you act.

shortcut.text: Ask {coworker} later what the warning was about.
shortcut.why: {coworker} may not have heard it fully either, and you need it before using the equipment.
shortcut.mis: A coworker's memory is as good as the original instructions.

fact: {coworker} says the plan is fine but crosses both arms and frowns.
issues.action: Ask {coworker} gently whether something about the plan seems off.
issues.reason: Body language that does not match the words often means an unspoken concern. Asking now may surface a real problem.
issues.lesson: Notice when body language and words do not match, and check in.

shortcut.text: Take {coworker} at their word, since they said the plan is fine.
shortcut.why: The crossed arms and frown suggest a concern. Ignoring the signal may leave a problem unspoken.
shortcut.mis: Only spoken words matter in a conversation.

fact: You missed the deadline {lead|the} mentioned for finishing the job.
clear: {Lead|the} wrote the ready time on the board.
issues.done: the ready time is already written on the board
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to confirm what time the job must be ready.
issues.reason: The deadline shapes how you plan the job. Confirming it now prevents a costly misunderstanding.
issues.lesson: Confirm key details you missed instead of guessing.

shortcut.text: Assume the job is due at the usual end-of-shift time.
shortcut.why: A rush job may have a different deadline. Guessing risks finishing too late.
shortcut.mis: The usual answer is probably the right one.

fact: {coworker2} keeps cutting in with side comments, and you are losing track of the steps.
issues.action: At the next pause, ask {lead|the} to recap the key steps.
issues.reason: A short recap fixes gaps caused by interruptions, and waiting for a pause is respectful.
issues.lesson: When interruptions break your understanding, politely ask for a recap.

shortcut.text: Nod along and figure out the steps once the work starts.
shortcut.brief: nod along and figure it out later
shortcut.why: Pretending to understand hides the gap until it causes a mistake.
shortcut.mis: Nodding along is the polite thing to do.

fact: {Lead|the} asks whether everyone understands the plan.
issues.action: Briefly summarize the plan back to {lead|the} to check you have it right.
issues.reason: Repeating the plan in your own words is the quickest way to catch a misunderstanding before work starts.
issues.lesson: Paraphrase instructions back to confirm you understood them.

shortcut.text: Say yes, since asking questions might slow everyone down.
shortcut.why: A quick yes skips the chance to catch a misunderstanding.
shortcut.mis: Saying you understand is the same as understanding.

proceed.text: Start the rush job the way {lead|the} described it.
proceed.why: You have the details you need, so starting the job as described is the right move.
proceed.lesson: Once you have heard and understood the instructions, act on them.

generic.text: Look at your phone during the huddle and catch up afterward.
generic.why: Not paying attention during instructions guarantees you will miss something.
generic.mis: You can catch up on instructions later.

generic.text: Interrupt {lead|the} mid-sentence to ask about something unrelated.
generic.why: Cutting in with an unrelated question breaks everyone's focus.
generic.mis: Any question is worth asking right away.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to repeat all of the instructions from the start.
overcaution.why: You already have the details. Asking for a full repeat holds up the whole team.
overcaution.mis: Hearing everything twice is always safer.

setup: {Lead|the} at {workplace|the} is about to explain a rush job to your team.

warning: Part of a warning about {equipment|the} was drowned out by noise.
time: You did not catch when the job is due.

steps.text: Ask to hear the warning again
Repeat the plan back in your own words

rel: You ask about what you missed once the explanation ends.
You ask about the missed detail after the explanation.
You can only repeat back what you have heard.
The warning has to be clear before work starts.
Your recap should include the ready time.
process.lesson: Listen first, clear up what you missed, confirm your understanding, then begin.

review.notes: Active listening and nonverbal cues; all issues occur during one huddle.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Tomorrow you will give a short spoken update about a change to {task|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have been asked to present a change to {task|the} at tomorrow's meeting.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody really listens to these updates anyway.
You have only tonight to prepare.
detail: You wrote your notes on index cards.
This is your first time presenting at work.

tiers.1: Getting a fact wrong in front of a group misleads everyone at once.
tiers.2: The time limit decides how much you can say.
tiers.3: Words the audience does not know make the message useless.
tiers.4: A setting where people cannot hear needs fixing before the content.
tiers.5: Slide design matters less than accuracy, timing and clarity.

fact: One number in your notes is from last month, and you are not sure it is still right.
clear: {coworker} confirmed this morning that the number is still current.
issues.action: Check that number with {coworker} or the records before you present it.
issues.reason: Presenting a wrong figure misleads everyone in the room. Checking it first protects your credibility.
issues.lesson: Verify the facts you plan to present before you speak.

shortcut.text: Leave the number in, since it is probably close enough.
shortcut.brief: keep the number as it is
shortcut.why: A wrong number spoken to a group spreads quickly and is hard to correct.
shortcut.mis: Numbers in a talk do not need to be exact.

fact: You have three minutes, but your notes would take about ten.
issues.short: notes that run three times too long
issues.action: Cut the update down to the three points people most need to know.
issues.brief: cut it to the three key points
issues.reason: Going over time loses the audience and the meeting. Choosing the key points makes the message stick.
issues.lesson: Fit your message to the time you have by focusing on what matters most.

shortcut.text: Plan to talk faster so everything fits into three minutes.
shortcut.why: Rushing makes the update harder to follow. Cutting content works better than speeding up.
shortcut.mis: Speaking faster lets you say more.

fact: Some of the audience will be {client.plural} who do not know the team's shorthand terms.
issues.action: Replace the shorthand terms with plain words everyone will know.
issues.brief: swap the shorthand for plain words
issues.reason: An audience cannot act on words it does not understand. Plain language reaches everyone in the room.
issues.lesson: Choose words that fit your audience, not just your team.

shortcut.text: Keep the shorthand, since it sounds more professional.
shortcut.why: Jargon the audience does not know sounds confusing, not professional.
shortcut.mis: Technical terms make a speaker sound more credible.

clear: You already replaced the shorthand terms with plain words.

fact: The meeting is in a noisy {area}, and there is no microphone.
clear: {Lead|the} already moved the meeting to a quiet room.
issues.done: the meeting was already moved to a quiet room
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} whether the meeting can move somewhere quieter.
issues.reason: A message nobody can hear accomplishes nothing. Fixing the setting makes everything else work.
issues.lesson: Make sure the setting lets your audience hear you.

shortcut.text: Plan to shout over the noise so everyone can hear.
shortcut.brief: plan to speak over the noise
shortcut.why: Speaking over loud noise strains your voice and still leaves people missing parts.

fact: Your one slide is packed with small text.
issues.action: Simplify the slide to a few large words that support what you say.
issues.reason: People cannot read small text and listen at the same time. A simple slide supports your words.
issues.lesson: Use visuals that support your talk rather than compete with it.

shortcut.text: Read the slide aloud word for word so nothing is missed.
shortcut.why: Reading a crowded slide aloud is slow and loses the audience.
shortcut.mis: Reading the slide is the safest way to present.

proceed.text: Give the update as planned, speaking clearly and looking at the group.
proceed.why: The content, timing and setting are ready, so delivering the update clearly is all that is left.
proceed.lesson: When the message is accurate and fits the audience, deliver it clearly and confidently.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to give the update for you.
generic.why: The update is your assignment. Handing it off without a reason avoids a useful skill.
generic.mis: Avoiding a presentation avoids the risk.

generic.text: Skip preparing and speak off the top of your head tomorrow.
generic.why: Unprepared talks ramble and miss key points.
generic.mis: Speaking naturally does not need preparation.

overcaution.text: Ask to postpone the update until next week to prepare more.
overcaution.why: The update is ready. Postponing delays information people need.

title: Your speaking notes
intro: These are your notes for tomorrow's three-minute update to staff and {client.plural}. Check them.
prompt: Which line of the notes is the problem?
doc.lesson: Good speaking notes are accurate, fit the time and use words the audience knows.

lines.text: Start: one sentence on why the change matters.
Point 1: what is changing about {task|the}, in plain words.
lines.fine: Uses plain language for a mixed audience.

bad.text: Point 1: explain the change using our internal codes and abbreviations.
bad.why: {client.plural} in the audience will not know internal codes. Plain words reach everyone.

lines.text: Point 3: who to ask with questions.
lines.fine: Tells the audience what to do next.

lines.text: Keep the whole update under three minutes.

bad.text: Add Points 4 through 9 with the full history of the old process.
bad.why: Six more points will not fit in a three-minute update and bury the three that matter.

lines.text: Look up from the notes and speak to the room.

bad.text: Read the notes word for word without looking up.
bad.why: Reading without looking up loses the audience's attention.

lines.text: End: ask whether there are any questions.

bad.text: End: leave right away without taking questions.

review.notes: Presenting and audience/setting; issues are all preparation-time facts.
